When speaking in Saint John, New Brunswick, on November 25, 1946, Mr. D. C. Coleman, the retired president of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, was quoted in the Telegraph-Journal as having said:
Any producing or trading centre is entitled to the advantages of its geographical location and its proximity to markets, but that railway rates cannot fairly be adjusted to relieve a centre of its geographical disadvantages.
If the word "areas" had been substituted for "centre" in this statement the east would be entitled to low rates resulting from water, highway and United States railway competition. But Mr. Coleman did not use the word "areas", because, by his doing so, the western provinces would be entitled to lower rates on account of the unchallengeable advantages of their location. Density of traffic, flat terrain which cuts operating expenses, and long hauls favour low rates for the prairies. Lack of water and highway competition on the plains, however, maintain rates at the maximum, and profits realized in that area go to make up losses in revenue in the central regions of Canada.
I say that because lower charges are forced upon the railways in central parts of Canada on account of the competition from other carriers. It has been repeatedly stated in the press that the suggested increase in rates would return $84 million in revenue to the railways. That is the sum of $7 million each month taken from the pockets of westerners and maritimers to assist the railways to operate more profitably. I say "westerners and maritimers" since other modes of transportation in central Canada will protect consumers there. In the west-and I must be pardoned for speaking from the western viewpoint, since I am more familiar with the situation there,-wholesalers, producers and manufacturers maintain that, under present freight rates in relation to present prices, their margin of profit is not large. They maintain that any increase in freight rates would certainly have to be followed by an authorization from the wartime prices and trade board for commodity price increases which would be added to consumer prices. Thus any increase in carrying charges, either now or in the future, is of vital concern to every farmer and wage-earner in the - west. The farmer will realize less income from the products he sells and, in turn, will find the costs of consumer goods considerably higher. The cost of living for all will appreciably increase.
A survey conducted by the Leader-Post of Regina, which in this instance rendered a service to everyone in the west, reveals that butter and poultry producers would suffer a loss of revenue exceeding $1 million yearly.
Increased charges for farm machinery would range upwards of a quarter of a million dollars a year. Live stock producers would have to pay out half a million dollars more in freight charges. Housewives would find their monthly store bills up at least five per cent. Hardware and lumber prices, already high, would climb substantially, and prove a further deterrent to prospective building.
In Regina alone it is estimated that building costs would increase by at least $100,000 a year. Prospective buyers of automobiles and trucks would have an average of $30 added to the price of each vehicle. Furniture, clothing and electrical appliances will all cost the consumer more. Wholesale grocers in the same city state that canned goods would carry an additional freight charge of forty-one cents per 100 pounds; and sugar, which has a rate of $1.41 per 100 pounds would be increased to $1.84 for the same quantity.
A few months ago an increase of thirteen cents an hour for steel workers was considered by Mr. Donald Gordon, chairman of the wartime prices and trade board, as likely to break the price ceiling, and was, in general effect, inflationary. So far, to my knowledge, there has been no comment offered by Mr. Gordon with regard to the effect of a general freight rate increase on the price structure of the country. If an increase of thirteen cents an hour to a few thousand steel workers is. in effect, inflationary, one must assume that increased freight charges which will increase commodity prices will make the holding of the price control line exceedingly difficult. Therefore any increase in freight charges contains a threat to the welfare of Canadians in all parts of the country.
There should be no attempt to be unfair to the railways. On the other hand, if an over-all increase in freight rates is discriminatory in effect it may have dangerous consequences. The imposition of an unfair and unwieldy freight structure upon any region of Canada can well develop an anti-confederation attitude. This has manifested itself on several occasions, both in the maritimes and in the west. This, of course, is to be avoided. All Canadians must remember that confederation should be based on equality and that economic discrimination against any area in the dominion may create separatist sentiments. I suggest that now is the opportune time to examine the whole freight rate structure so as to remove existing inequalities. Now is the time to set up a royal commission, if you will, to investigate thoroughly all charges of discrimination which have been levelled against the railways by western and other organiza-
The Address-Mr. McKay

tions. I submit that, until this whole matter is ironed out to the satisfaction of both the west and the maritimes, no body is in any position to appraise the need for a general increase in railway rates of any kind.
I have already referred to the accounting system employed by the railways; but, leaving that for the moment, I wish to draw the attention of the house to another situation. The war years brought enormous industrial development to this nation. Even though we are now at peace, there continues to be an increased income from trade. It is to be hoped that this improved state in our economy will provide much more revenue for our transportation system than in pre-war days.
Again referring to the accounting systems of the railways, I question the method which makes heavy charges against operations to provide huge reserves. It was reported in the Toronto Daily Star of January 3, 1947, that Canadian Pacific reserves had increased to $332 million by the end of 1945, and this after paying dividends for 1944 and 1945 of almost $42 million. Moreover, according to the bulletin "Railways of Canada 1945", issued by the Department of Trade and Commerce, the depreciation reserves, deferred maintenance and other contingencies funds of the combined railways of Canada had reached the huge total of $493,963,000 by the close of 1945. It may be safely assumed that these figures are substantially higher today. This fact should be carefully considered when one is examining the financial position of our railways.
In so far as the Canadian National Railways is concerned, one must view with alarm the enormous overhead of this railway. The government railway has never had an opportunity to operate on the right side of the ledger except during war time, and that situation has not been owing to inadequacy of either passenger or freight revenue. If adjustments were made to the capital structure under which this system labours I question very much if there would be any demand from this source for an increase in rates of any kind. The Canadian National Railways was organized from bankrupt, privately owned lines with impossible capital debts. No railway in America carries the burden of debt which the government-operated railway bears. No privately operated railroad anywhere would have assumed the liabilities foisted upon the national system by past federal administrations. Generosity, presumably to friends of governments then in power, apparently dictated the policies of those days.
fMr. McKay.]
The bondholders and shareholders were in most cases well provided for. Now, when deficits occur because of an unwieldy and unfair debt overhead, all Canadians are forced to contribute to the bondholders of defunct private enterprise railways, either through raids on the public treasury or by increased railway carrying charges.
The first railway to fail was the Grand Trunk Pacific, which was followed by the Canadian Northern and others. The accumulated debt of these bankrupt privately owned roads amounted to well over $1,200 million. No one has yet explained why these bankrupt enterprises were not taken over at face value, at so many cents on the dollar. There should have been a revaluation of stock as would have been done in private business.
While the hodgepodge of privately constructed railways was being integrated into an efficient national system, the United States railways were undergoing a reorganization of a different kind. Many United States railways went into the hands of receivers and debts were reduced as much as fifty per cent. No such financial reorganization occurred with the government railways with the consequence that prior to the war this system was unable to meet the interest charges on its more than a billion dollar debt.
Some relief was granted in 1937, it is true, when the Capital Revision Act wiped out loans granted by the government to meet operating deficits. Previously such loans were added to capital debt. The same act changed government loans for capital purposes prior to 1932 to equity capital which meant that interest was paid by the Canadian National only in years of declared surplus. Even with these adjustments, interest charges were still twenty-eight per cent of gross revenue, while the Canadian Pacific rates were seventeen per cent, and that of class 1 United States railways was sixteen per cent. There was obviously no attempt to place the government railway on a comparative basis with any other railway. It seems apparent that, unless the government writes down the Canadian National Railways capital debt structure, this railway cannot ever be profitably operated, regardless of freight and other rates charged. I appeal to the government to assume directly some of the liabilities charged against the Canadian National Railwas's so that the system may have a square deal. If this adjustment is not made the state operated railways are handicapped so as to preclude a proper comparison with railways operating under

The Address-Mr. Merritt
private ownership. The efficiency of operating personnel is defeated by unreasonable and unfair overhead.
Included in the national system is the Intercolonial railway which serves the maritimes. Just a brief word about this railway. The Intercolonial railway was built for political rather than for economic reasons. It was intended to cement the maritimes into the confederation block and to be as far removed from the United States border as was feasible. This may have served a strategic purpose a half century ago, but it created a long freight haul to and from the maritimes. The alleviation from excessively high freight rates over this route received some consideration in the 1927 Maritime Freight Rates Act. The effect of this legislation should have been to place the maritime areas on an equal footing with central Canada. However, the application of maximum charges set forth in the act still militates against the provinces down by the sea. Central Canada has efficient highway competition which forces charges down below the maximum permitted; therefore the differential existing prior to 1927 is, in effect, practically unchanged.
May I commend to the government the facts just presented. In order to appreciate thoroughly the effects of the present rate structure and the possibility of an increase to the west and the maritimes, a careful study should be made of all facts pertaining thereto. An examination of the effects of the whole freight rate structure upon our economic life should be ascertained. It is my opinion that freight rates for essential goods should be held to a minimum. Moreover, there must not be regional discrimination. Should periods occur when operating expenses exceed revenues the nation as a whole should be responsible for the deficits. All parts of Canada should assume a part of that burden if it should occur. The future welfare of Canada as a nation might well be at stake if rates are to vary in different parts of the country. Moreover, it is time that the railways' dependence on the west for top operating revenue stopped. Until now the west has carried the major load in providing the railways with profits. Easterners, when apprised of this truth, will, I am sure, join with us in demanding that the federal government assume responsibility for an equalization of the freight rate burden, so that the extremities of this nation, the western provinces on the one hand and the maritimes on the other, may receive the square deal to which they are entitled.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in this debate we are discussing an amendment expressing want of confidence in this government, and I am sorry that I do not see in the house tonight many ministerial targets for my remarks. I shall have to content myself with my good friend the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie), for whom I have a special message this evening.
First, however, I wish to make a short reference to the withdrawal of the Canadian army of occupation from Europe and to the bearing of that on the amendment which has been moved by my leader.
This afternoon we heard quoted the statement of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in 1945, when he said that the army of occupation as then planned was modest, having regard to our direct interest in world peace. With that statement in mind, Mr. Speaker, I say to you that the withdrawal of that force can only mean that Canada ceased to contribute to the discharge of her direct responsibility which goes with that direct interest. The reason given at the time was administrative difficulties. I wish to say to the house and particularly to the government that that reason fooled no one at the time and it fools no one now. There would not have been a reference to this matter from this side of the house had it not been for the attempt to base this withdrawal on a question of principle. I think that attempt was exploded by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) this afternoon, if indeed it needed exploding, because actually I think it blew back on him who attempted to put it forward.
What are the facts and the very simple facts? At the end of the war we had in Europe an army of occupation, consisting of approximately one division. It included many long-service men, men who had fought through most of the fighting and who were being kept, for the time being, in that army of occupation against their will. It is obvious that the government could not have left those men over there doing that duty when there were short-service men at home. It is obvious too that this government would not send replacements over to take the place of these long-service men. That is the beginning and the end of the mystery of the army of occupation. That was the administrative difficulty and I say to you tonight, Mr. Speaker, that it was a difficulty of political expediency and that only, and it is no use trying to make out anything else.
I wish to say to the government, too, and particularly to the Minister of National
The Address-Mr. Merritt

Defence (Mr. Claxton), who, I am sorry, is not in his seat at the moment, that in his recently expressed concern for the hearth and home of the Canadian soldier I believe he misjudges young Canadians. The young Canadian soldier does not like separation from his home. Who does? Nobody does. But the interest of all the young men of this country is in the future of their country first and in the future of their sons and their sons' sons, and it is not in any temporary disagreeable circumstances that they must put up with if they are to lead Canada on to the great future that is undoubtedly before us as a nation. I say to the government, with all the seriousness at my command, that if the absence of a few young men in Canada's service from Canada now would make any contribution to the cause of world peace in the future many young Canadians would go to the ends of the earth and stay there if this government had the fortitude to ask them so to do. If it comes to a choice between principle and expediency there never has been much doubt in the minds of the Canadian people what course this government would take.
Take national defence, for instance. On February 12 in this house, the Prime Minister reiterated the pledge he gave to President Roosevelt and indeed to the Canadian people that there was an obligation on Canada to do everything in her power to defend herself from attack from without and to prevent any aggressor from moving across Canadian soil against our great neighbour to the south. Contrast that statement of our obligation with the provision which this government has made for national defence.
Take management-labour relations. The whole history of management-labour relations under this government has been one of inability to attempt -to enforce the law as it stood at any one time, again because of the political inexpediency of so doing. Or take the socialist legislation of which we have seen many an example during this session. Is this really a Liberal party opposite us, Mr. Speaker? That is what I think many people in Canada want to know. These are some of the reasons why we lack confidence in this government.
Take housing, and I wish to devote the rest of my remarks to that subject. We had a statement from the Minister of Reconstruction (Mr. Howe) on housing early in this debate, and I desire to congratulate him and the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie) on being the only two ministers who have made statements of government policy since we assembled here in January, although much time has been taken up by members on this

side asking for such statements. The Minister of Reconstruction at least made a statement, and he took great pride in the fact that there had been built in Canada last year 60,000 houses and that his target for 1947 was 80,000. He can take what comfort he likes out of that, but to do so looks to me very much like pulling oneself up by one's bootstraps. Simply to meet this self-imposed quota will not do very much to house the people in this country who need homes so badly. What has been the government's policy of which they are so proud and which was to produce 60,060 houses? The priority system has been a joke. Less than twenty per cent of the houses built in Canada have been built with priority assistance. Large industrial orders have taken most of the remainder of the building material that has been produced. The private builder has had to scramble to get any material and yet he has built over eighty per cent of Canada's houses. Shortly put, that is the result of the government's housing policy.
I wish to test that by two further facts. I hold in my hand an extract of the Maclean building reports, as quoted in the Financial Post. It shows that in the ten months of 1946, up to November 1, the proportion of residential building in 1946 as compared with non-residential building has fallen 15-1 per cent since 1945. That is a pretty good gauge of what the housing policy of this government has brought about. For three years before the war the proportion of housing to industrial production has been over fifty per cent, and this year it has dropped to 39'6 per cent. Then again, testing it by the same report on the total construction contracts awarded in Canada, I find that engineering contracts increased 212 per cent over 1945; commercial and industrial contracts increased 123-5 per cent over 1945; industrial contracts increased 102-7 per cent over 1945 and, if you please, residential construction contracts awarded increased 8-9 per cent. That will give the house some idea of the way in which this government distributes building material.
Even if there were completed the 60,000 houses in 1946, in my own city of Vancouver in the twelve months of 1946 there were actually fewer houses completed than were completed in 1945. That took place in a city which is growing faster than any other city in Canada and which has a housing shortage that I have every reason to believe is the worst in the country. We built fewer houses in 1946 than we did in 1945.
I now turn to the question of stimulation of building material which was the real job of the government, instead of fooling around with

The Address-Mr. Merritt
priorities and things like that. What has happened? Last April the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply took over the job of stimulating building material. We had been asking him to do so for a year but it had not been done. However he started a year late, and I believe he has worked hard. What did he find he had to do in order to stimulate building material? He has had to give price reliefs from the price ceiling; he has had to give incentive subsidies to get increased production; he has had to reverse the taxation policy by giving double depreciation; he has had to make loans for capital development. The people presumably have been taxed so hard that they have not the money for that purpose. He has had to give guaranteed markets to some firms before they had confidence enough in the government's policies to increase their output. And after a great newspaper campaign he finally got around-and I think this was a year and a half late-to pulling down the Debert camp and other big camps and distributing that building material where it should have gone a long time before. Despite taking these heroic measures to stimulate the building materials-and certainly I consider reversing the government's policy an heroic measure-what is the fact now? We have heard from Vancouver and Toronto in the last two days that there is an acute shortage of nails and that houses cannot be finished because of that.
The production of nails in 1946 was down fifteen per cent over 1945, despite the government's attempt to stimulate the market. I know hon. gentlemen opposite will say that there was a big steel strike last year. That is true, and it was the chief cause of the diminution in the production of nails. But whose responsibility is it for good management-labour relations if it is not the responsibility of the government? Anyone who sat on the industrial committee last year knows that strike could have been settled at 13J cents an hour, or whatever figure it was settled at, on the first day of the strike. If the government was going to reverse its policy and go over the ten cent limit it was not necessary to keep the steel workers out for eighty days and thereby slow down the production of nails. That is a simple answer to that shortage. I hope that the people of Canada who are suffering from a shortage of nails will know it stems back to the weak policy of the government in dealing with a great management-labour problem.
There is one more thing I wish to add on the general subject of housing, and that has to do with low-rent housing. In the minister's 83166-71
statement earlier in the debate, he laid down the policy of the government as opposed to the introduction of low-rent housing. By that I mean municipal corporations assisted by both provincial and dominion governments bringing about low rental housing for those in the low-income groups and to those living in slum dwellings. I wish to say to the government that if that is their policy it is completely unrealistic.
I hold in my hand a voluminous report of the Vancouver Housing Association which made a detailed and intelligent survey in my own city before the war and brought it up to date in 1945. They have no doubts about the need for low rental housing for the lower income group. There are very few social, public or municipal bodies in the country, except this government, which have any doubts on that score. Knowing conditions as I do in my own city and constituency, I say the minister's suggestion that we can get along under the "filtering up" process is so unrealistic as to be unworthy of a man whom I consider to be realistic.
Finally, I wish to turn to the question which has been discussed several times in the house, and particularly yesterday and today, namely the administration of housing under the Veterans Land Act, the small holdings. There is no question that the way in which the small holdings project or progiamme has developed in Canada in the last two years amounts to a public scandal.
In this debate we have heard from the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy), who has told us about the Sarnia and Windsor houses; we have heard the minister; we have heard from the hon. member from Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) with regard to the Braefoot subdivision; we have heard from the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) and the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Miller) about the Charleswood project, and yesterday we heard about the wartime housing project in the Louth subdivision near St. Catharines. I wish to call the attention of the house to the fact that the conditions in all of these subdivisions across the country are the same. In every case there is bad workmanship; in every case drainage apparently has not been thought of at all; in every case there has been bad material delivered to the job and apparently also in one case short material. In every case the veteran has ended up with being charged an excessive cost for the work which was done, and a cost which was very much over what he was led to believe, by the government pamphlets, he would be charged for one of these houses.

The Address-Mr. Merritt

I just wish to add my little song to that of the other members on this side of the house. I have an example from Lulu island near Vancouver, in the Veterans Land Act subdivision there, which I have called to the attention of the minister. This was the case of a veteran who was wounded overseas, who has a wife and child and whose wife was expecting another. Last June he bought his house and the contract price was $5,861.22. This winter he has had to vacate his house. There were eight inches of water under it. His septic tank was leaking and flooding the land. Two houses away, the whole top of a septic tank simply floated off, and brought about such a condition in the area that the veteran had to vacate and go into the town. His wife went to stay with her parents and he went to stay with his, both of them sleeping on couches in the living room.

Yes, I am well aware that the director of the Veterans Land Act took up this case. The minister was kind enough to send me the report, which suggested that the flooding conditions were not serious; and I answered the minister on that score.
I have in my hand two photographs. I wish that Hansard were an illustrated document, but I will try to illustrate to the house what these photographs show. One of them shows "the back of the house which I have." You can see the reflections of two telephone poles in the water and the water is covered with ripples, there being on this day quite a wind. I would not call that just dampness, and I doubt if the house would. Then I have another photograph, which is of "my next door neighbour's place, and it was nearly as bad as my own." There you can see not only the reflection of the telephone pole but the reflection of the whole house in the water; and you can trace perfectly clearly in the water the reflection of a ladder which lies against the side of the house and which may have been used to climb from the boat into the house. Those are serious conditions, and are not such as could warrant the director's characterization of this situation as being not serious. It seems to me that anyone who does

not live in such a place should at least withhold comment on the "relative" seriousness of the flooding of one's basement.

to the minister. I just outlined that case to show that there is hardly a place in Canada where these same conditions do not exist.
I now wish to refer to the minister's speech. He ended up yesterday by referring to our main interest in the veterans. He made promises to repair the damage and expressed his desire for the cooperation of all members of the house and the hope that we would be satisfied with his frankness with us yesterday. I can assure him of the cooperation of every member of this party. We raise this matter only because it must be raised and must be settled, and he has our full cooperation. We appreciate his frankness. We know that the minister personally has every good wish toward the veterans and would do anything in his power to assist their cause; but those good wishes are not enough and the minister's speech is not enough. We need results as well as good wishes with respect to these Veterans Land Act projects.
I am now going to outline some of the results we hope to attain before we stop talking about these matters. We want the following assurances from the minister, from the point of view of the veteran. First, we want to be assured that all these houses will be put back in proper repair. I think he has given us that assurance. We want

The Address-Mr. Merritt
to be assured further that the drainage problem will be attacked immediately and successfully and not at the cost of any of the veterans on any of these projects. Those are the first things upon which we want the most positive assurances. We do not want to wait, as one correspondent of mine suggested, ten years before a municipality can get certain pumps and thereby drain the low-lying land. We want these houses fixed so that the men can live in them now. We want the most energetic steps taken at once.
Second, we want the assurance-and this is particularly important-that no veteran who has a house in bad repair or with bad drainage is called upon to sign a contract until he has satisfied himself that the house has been repaired so that he can keep it as his home and be proud of it in the future. This is a most important point, because it is my information that in the Charleswood project veterans have been given until May 1 to sign these contracts for these houses, even although they are not fully repaired, or else they must vacate. That attitude on the part of the officials of the minister's department, if it is correctly described, is not, I think, the one the minister himself would adopt toward any veteran. So we want that matter looked into and an assurance given us that that kind of thing will not occur. There have been other cases of pressure by officers of the Veterans Land Act division of the minister's department, pressure to sign up originally, pressure to hurry up and make a choice. We have much evidence of that kind of thing, and we want the minister to look personally into the question of what pressure is being put upon these veterans.

I wish to make particular reference to the remarks of the director, in the case I referred to the minister. In addition to suggesting that this "lake" was not seriously flooding, he also suggested that perhaps the veteran had acted with too great haste in accepting this house, and that, after all, the veteran had not been able to provide himself with a house from any other source. If that is the attitude of the director I say I believe it is the duty of the minister to have that attitude corrected. The veteran has no responsibility whatever for the fact that he is without housing accommodation. It is not his fault that he cannot get a house on his own resources, and that 83166-71i
sort of statement does not give me confidence in the eventual happy settlement of these difficulties under this administration.

speechtext: Yes, I shall be very glad to do so; I have some here. It seems to be thought by some of the officials of this department that, as to these veterans who have flooded or badly constructed houses, the principle of caveat emptor applies; that these veterans, having bought the houses, must take them as they are and suffer the consequences. I want to say to the minister that in the circumstances in which this small holdings scheme under the land act was born and introduced to the veterans who came back from overseas, there is a great responsibility on the government, as I think the Minister of Veterans Affairs appreciates, to lean over backwards in seeing to it that these veterans get every possible break, and even more breaks than they would have been given in an ordinary commercial contract. The very fact that they were contracting with the government which said it owed them such an obligation was likely to make them less careful in regard to the business details; and if a house was recommended to them by a government official, many of these men would not think it necessary to make any inquiries themselves before signing up. I think there is a great paternal obligation on the government to people settled in these subdivisions.

speechtext: Would the hon. member not admit that any of these cases which have been brought to the attention of the department have been looked into right away and rectified if at all possible?

Yes; I want to assure the minister and his parliamentary assistant that I personally have had every courtesy from both hon. gentlemen in regard to these matters, but I am talking of the way things sift down across this wide country; and it does appear to me that there is need to jack up the administration under the Veterans' Land Act. My goodness, it is perfectly clear to everybody that there is a need for this. Bad workmanship; floods; choice of location-these are not the results that flow from competent management.
There is a third assurance we want from the minister; that is, that the excessive costs of these homes will not have to be borne by
The Address-Mr. Merritt

the veterans. As to that I wish first to refer to the resolution of the veterans affairs committee contained in its final report of July 25 of last year; it is recommendation No. 2, on page 6:
That the government give consideration to the introduction of a bill to amend the Veterans' Land Act, 1942, to provide that the total cost of all homes over six thousand dollars presently constructed or in actual process of construction under the small holdings scheme be subsidized twenty-three and one-third per cent.
I hope we may be assured by the minister that effect will be given to this recommendation now. Then I want to ask the minister to see to it that a revaluation is made of all these damaged and flooded houses. I say these houses were built on a cost plus management fee basis; that they are now damaged goods, and that you cannot expect to get cost plus fixed fees for damaged goods. Even if they are repaired, in many cases they will not be as suitable for the veteran as they would have been otherwise. Each house should be revalued to make sure the veteran is not called upon to pay more than he should for it.
I want to make the second point, that in this revaluation any consequential damage which has been suffered by the purchaser through no fault of his own should be taken into account in fixing the final price. To mention again the case I referred to the minister, in order to give him my idea of consequential damage, that veteran went on the land last summer, ploughed it and paid for the ploughing. His wife bought curtains, carpets and so on to fit that house, together with many other household accessories that go only with the house in which you are living, as many hon. members know. These are consequential damages, for which that man should be reimbursed. In the case in point the veteran concerned is now being given a wartime house and his deposit on the house under the Veterans' Land Act has been returned, so that his case is dead except as an example, but for this consequential damage. In his new wartime house, however, he has lost the value of his ploughing, his curtains and so on, and is suffering considerable inconvenience for which, under a commercial contract, he would be reimbursed. I think that should be taken into account in the revaluation. It is not as though caveat emptor applied; it is not as though he knew the house was going to be flooded. On the facts as related to me he did not know that. The local officials knew it, however, because, when the house was being built the previous winter, men could not get in to work on the place for several days,

and all the neighbours were surprised when this man moved into the place. Apparently that was a disability within the knowledge of the department and not within the knowledge of the veteran, so that I do not believe he should suffer for that.
From the point of view of the taxpayer, hon. members on this side of the house would like certain requirements met. The first is that all necessary repairs shall be done at the expense of the contractors. The minister said that was being looked into. I understand that in most government contracts there is a "sound workmanship" clause. It seems to me the things we have heard about cannot be considered sound workmanship, and must be in breach of contract. The general public should not be called upon to pay for those repairs. Then, by order in council last year, with the approval of the veterans affairs committee, $1,000,000 was applied to this project. We should like to know whether that floated away with the top of the septic tank, or what happened to it, and why it has not reduced the cost to the veterans.

I simply suggest that we should like to know.
Then I believe we should cut out these cost plus fixed fee contracts, and I shall give my reason for that. I have a case here of one of the Braefoot houses, which was worked out at a cost per square foot of $8.14. Last summer, in the debate on housing, the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply gave the National Housing Act figure as $4.20 per square foot, with an increase of ten per cent last year. So that apparently under the National Housing Act, in calculating lending value, one is allowed $4.62 per square foot and this house cost $8.14 per square foot. 1 had some figures from Vancouver for private housing at $6 per square foot. I believe 1 have said enough to show what is wrong with a cost plus management fee contract.
What we want is that the government shall not simply say, "Oh it was very hard; we could not get good materials; we could not get good workmen." They had good materials to make munitions of war; they had good workmen to make munitions of war. I am sorry to say I cannot accept that excuse for the bad workmanship in these projects. Good inspection-the inspection upon which the government insists under the National Housing Act-would have obviated every bit of this.

The Address-Mr. Maybank
A letter from the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) in September, 1945, called the danger of bad drainage to the attention of the department. Therefore there could have been no reason why that was not properly looked after. I believe the taxpayers should know that any sum of money they have to pay, which is not paid by the contractors, is the responsibility of the government.
I realize I have only a short time left to speak, but with the time at my disposal I would refer to the suggestion for a royal commission. The minister has said that a royal commission would do no good because it would keep people waiting for a year to have repairs done. We do not want a royal commission before the repairs are done; we want that to go ahead at top speed. But what we do want a royal commission to do is to see that these financial adjustments, of which I have spoken, are carried out, and to see that the mess in connection with these projects does not fall on the veteran, and that it does not fall on the taxpayers any more than it must.
My final word is this, that against the failures of this government in housing, labour relations, foreign affairs, tax reductions and many other things which hon. members have mentioned, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in this debate took pride in the fact that forty per cent of the voters of Canada voted for his party and government during the recent by-election. I say to him, Mr. Speaker, that it is high time we got rid of a government which prides itself on forty per cent efficiency.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad that this evening and on other occasions the question of freight rates, in a general way, has been discussed. And in a "general" way I also wish to enter into discussion of the freight rate structure of the country, from the viewpoint of its being "generally" an inequitable structure.
It is true I may have occasion to remark something about an application which is now before the transport board. But any reference to the application before the board is, as authors so often say in their introductory words in books, purely coincidental.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Obiler dictum.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I would repeat what the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) has said, that he hopes that all such remarks will be obiter dicta-and I believe that means in the nature of an aside or asides. I suppose any references I would make would be obiter dicta.
So that at least the Minister of Transport and I start out in complete agreement at the present time, although some little time back we were in disagreement on a point of order.
But before touching upon the freight rates question, I wish to make one other remark- but shortly-upon a different subject. My first observation shall be to compliment and congratulate the government upon the agreements thus far made relating to interprovincial and intergovernmental settlement of finances. I believe the government is to be highly complimented upon the progress it has thus far been able to make.
I have been reading the speech from the throne from Queen's Park, and there would appear to be some disagreement in that quarter as to the adequacy of the proposals of the dominion government. But whether they agree with the adequacy of the proposals or not, I think people in all provinces must realize that some changes had to be made in the financial set-up in Canada, and the load placed upon the provinces having the opportunity to get the wherewithal to carry the load. I believe all must realize that the poorer provinces could not carry their load; and this is particularly true in my own province which, from a tax collector's point of view, is too poor to go ahead with such developments as are necessary and to effect necessary social amenities, although it does create a great deal of wealth. But from the point of view of the tax collector, and including only direct taxation, it must be regarded as a poor province. For that reason, and because a settlement greatly beneficial to it was made possible, I believe the government is entitled to great credit.
But when paying tribute to the government for a job well done, I do not want to overlook one man who played a great part in these dominion-provincial negotiations and whose work in no small measure contributed to their success. I refer to the Hon. Stuart Garson, premier of Manitoba. I have sometimes thought he was the most far-sighted of any of those who gathered about the table. I do not press that comparison; but he certainly was clear-sighted, patient, conciliatory and resourceful in negotiating for his province. And, above all, he was sincere-and that is important. He was sincere in trying to work out something that would be for the benefit of all Canada, while working especially for his own province. It is my belief that he is responsible for a large measure of the success attained.
But now, just when we have concluded satisfactory interim agreements which will put the
The Address-Mr. Maybank

provinces upon a better situation henceforward, we in western Canada face a serious threat to our economy, and I believe the same is true of the maritimes. However I speak more particularly with respect to the prairies.
A special endeavour is being made by certain agencies in the country to place an additional tax on the backs of the people of western Canada. It is a scheme peculiarly designed to tax them, and only them; and if it succeeds it will go far to undo a great deal of the good that has been accomplished in the proposals contained in the agreements I have mentioned.
Mr. Speaker, I know that the difficulty of determining a point of order in the house with reference to a discussion of freight rates is extremely difficult. I am, and I think all hon. members are, deeply sensible of the hard position you have to fill. I am-and I believe this view is shared by all other hon. members- keenly sensible of the excellent manner in which you discharge your function as Speaker in endeavouring to keep us within the limits laid down by the rules. Certainly I do not wish to offend against the ruling handed down by Your Honour through Mr. Deputy Speaker last night in relation to this subject. If I do mention the proposals before the transport board I wish you to know now that it is done only for the purpose of leading up to a conclusion and recommendation I have to make, and independent of what happens to be before a court at the present time.
I had occasion a little earlier this evening to discuss the exact case that is before the board, and I would recall to you that the case before the board is expressed in these words-I am leaving out certain interconnected words in order to get it more clearly-"the railway association applies under section 325 and certain other sections for authority to make an advance of thirty per cent in tolls and rates." That is the only question before the transport board. There is nothing before that board at the present time about grain rates because I think it is made clear that since grain rates are statutory, they do not come within the purview of the jurisdiction of the board. So they could be discussed. By the same token, increases of thirty-one per cent or thirty-five per cent or ninety-two per cent are not before the board. All that is before the board is a thirty per cent increase, a very narrow sort of application-a narrow field from which we must keep away.
I should like to introduce with this comment what I am going to say. Sometimes, when one is discussing what will be the effect of a judgment, he does not need to enter into a discussion as to what the judgment ought to be.

You may discuss the effect of a judgment without saying anything about the merits or demerits of the arguments pro and con which lead up to the judgment. If there were a murder trial going on in Ottawa I feel that we would agree that we should not discuss the merits of the case for the prosecution or for the defence. Whether the accused should be convicted or not is something that we would feel we had no right to discuss. But the effect of being found guilty and hanged is that after you are hanged you are dead. There would be no prohibition upon our discussing the effect of hanging.
With reference to this freight rate application, I may say that, while all the railroads are making it, I think it can be viewed chiefly as a Canadian Pacific application. Most of the railroads with the exception of the Canadian National are small, but the Canadian National situation is not important in connection with freight rate making. That is a point that I may develop a little later. It is something which has been pretty well accepted over the years in rate-making circles, that the Canadian National and its needs are not to be taken as the criteria. So one may say that this is pretty well a Canadian Pacific proposition.

speechtext: You are not serious about that?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I am quite serious. It
will be recalled that the application has been made not to raise certain uneconomic rates, not to seek an increase by having cost saving schemes made effective; it is simply an application that everything be raised thirty per cent. I think, in regard to coal, a specific figure is asked for. By reason of the inequitable situation in which we find ourselves today in connection with the rate structure, a demand of that kind is levelled particularly at western Canada. There can be no doubt that the allowance of such an increase will be permissive. I do not say what the judgment of the board ought to be, but I do say that, in the event of a judgment permitting the increase, the railroads ought to take counsel together and with the government before they put it into effect. I suggest that such a remark is apt in the case because the Canadian National Railways is our own creature. Before the Canadian National Railways actually increases rates, there ought tfi be a conference to consider the effect of that raise before they take advantage of any judgment that may be rendered in their favour. I do not speak as to the merits of the judgment itself, but the railroads, particu-

The Address-Mr. Maybank
larly the one which is ours, ought to consider the situation carefully before taking advantage of any judgment.
I have said that, by reason of the inequitable system under which we labour at the present time with rates as they are, any change will necessarily bear rather heavily upon us in western Canada. Some other speakers have already pointed this out. If the railroads have the power at any time to raise rates, they will not raise them in central Canada but will raise them in western Canada. I do not suggest by this statement, any moral obliquity on the part of the Canadian railways; it is simply a matter of fact that when it is possible to raise rates by reason of a judgment they raise them in western Canada because western Canada is a natural monopoly. The contrary holds Lrue here in the east. There is no monopoly, there is water competition, and there is good truck competition here.
If any person has any doubt about this I ask him to note what has appeared in the newspapers, and then I think he will be convinced that what I am saying is correct. The newspapers do not report any person appearing before the transport board at the present time for either Ontario or Quebec, although an application is being made for an increase "straight across the board".

and I thank the hon. member for New Westminster for adding a punch to what I was saying. It is most significant that people should be faced with an apparent thirty per cent increase and not care. Since I have been interrupted by a Scotsman, helpfully I admit, I am reminded of what happened in Glasgow.

speechtext:
I agree that the hon. member is a Canadian, and a very good one. However I know he will not take umbrage in being reminded that until a short time ago he was Scotch. As I was saying, the action taken by the governments of Ontario and
Quebec reminds me of the people of Glasgow. They had a municipal railway in Glasgow and the city fathers raised the rates. There was no protest. The city fathers raised the rates again, and still there was no protest. The city fathers raised the rates again, and there was no protest. After a short time, despite the fact there had been no protest, the city fathers lowered the rates one notch. Then there was a protest. All the citizens of Glasgow came forward complaining bitterly of the reduction and demanding that the rate should be put back at the high spot in order that they might save more money by walking.
Here in the central provinces the position is like that. It does not make any difference whether the rates are raised or not because the people would save money by not using the railroads, and so the companies will not do it. There cannot be any doubt, on the other hand, that any threat of this sort is a gun aimed at western Canada and, if permission to increase is granted, the gun will go off. Moreover, we are at the present time in the position of having, on the whole, about a fifteen per cent higher level of freight rates in western Canada than exists in central Canada, and so far as British Columbia is concerned the level is about twenty-five per cent higher; so that any increase which is granted, say thirty-one per cent, would be thirty-one per cent on SI in the central provinces, thirty-one per cent on SI.15 on the prairies, and thirty-one per cent on SI .25 farther west, and whereas we have already an inequitable system, the same percentage applied to different bases would naturally increase the discrimination, which is something that, as we look ahead, causes a great deal of concern.
I know a certain business institution in Manitoba with an annual freight bill, on outgoing goods, of SI,250,000 and, on incoming products, about S400.000, or a total of about $1,650,000. Half a million dollars added to that would be a great addition to the expense of doing business. Its competitor at the present time, a large competitor in the central provinces, has a freight bill which compares with the Manitoba company's bill as six compares with twelve. If the increase is granted you have in the one case a percentage increase on twelve and in the other case an increase on six. You see the great disparity that at once occurs, and that applies on everything. It is so with a pound of rice; it is so with a binder; it is so with a tractor, with a pair of shoes and a pair of shoe laces. It applies to everything. I do not know of anything that could be more inflationary than a freight rate increase. Suppose that by reason of trans-
The Address-Mr. Maybank

portation costs the cost of an article increases by one cent. In small towns, particularly mining towns, the retailer will naturally nearly always add a nickel to the price of the goods, and when that is done on every single article that people are using the effect is very inflationary indeed.
I do not think any person has yet adequately presented the difficulties in which the railroads find themselves, and I am not adequately presenting their difficulties. I am willing to take on faith that the railroads will need some kind of relief. The only point which I should like all members of the house and all people in the country to consider is just what sort of relief ought to be granted.
There is one thing I should like to warn against. Some of the protagonists for the railroads, in saying that they need some relief, would attempt to make out of their position a sort of wage claim. I know one advocate of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, speaking at a public meeting somewhere, indicated that the freight rate question was just a wage claim. Frankly, I regard that sort of propaganda with a good deal of suspicion. I am not forgetting that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company was the only employer that did not deal generously with its employees who got tangled up in the 1919 general strike, and I am not forgetting that every effort to get them to act in the same manner as other employers was fruitless. I am not forgetting that, when they were asked to acquiesce and assist in a general inquiry into the position they had taken with respect to their employees, they turned a deaf ear to that request. The request was made by the Minister of Labour of this government (Mr. Mitchell) but the C.P.R. would have none of it, and so, when they talk about their needs in terms of the needs of their workmen, I cannot help viewing their propaganda with a good deal of suspicion.
I have dealt already with the general inequity that exists in freight rates in the country, and I wish to sav that there are a good many reasons why the prairie provinces, and British Columbia too, should not be paying to the railroad economy of Canada more than they have already, over the years, been paying. I was reminded this afternoon by a right hon. gentleman of this house that our freight rate structure has never been scientifically devised. Like Topsy it has just growed. One time a long time ago a rate was fixed and that rate became the datum. I am sure the Minister of Transport will agree with me that they used that one rate as a datum,

and from that moved on to another rate. We have never really had a scientific investigation of our freight rate structure.

speechtext: All the traffic would bear.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
For a long time-and this was borne out by the statements of the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Winkler) a night or so ago-it would indeed appear that the charges were often levied on the basis of what they could get the shipper to pay; in other words, on whatever the traffic would bear. I think the rates should be set basically on the costs of doing business and if, when the rates have been fixed in that way, taking into consideration all things, some part of the country cannot get railroad service on the rates so levied, some method of relief must be worked out because, being the political entity that we are, we must see that decent railroad service is provided everywhere. But the first consideration should be the cost of doing business.
It costs a good deal less to operate a railroad in western Canada than it does anywhere else. This was brought out most clearly in hearings before the board in the 1920's. I shall have something to say a little later about the need of using stale figures in presenting an argument in this house. In 1925, 1926 and 1927 and perhaps some other years, the province of Manitoba was represented by H. J. Symington, K.C., in various hearings. He is now president of Trans-Canada Air Lines and a director of the Canadian National Railways. Under a searching examination, resulting from years of research and a natural acumen and aptitude for this sort of inquiry, he brought out a great many facts respecting our railroad problem, particularly as it relates to western Canada. Those inquiries showed that western Canada supplied to the railroads the major part of their net revenue. It did then and it does now. I made extensive notes of the transcript of proceedings taken at that time. I do not mean that I did it at that time; I have done it since. For example, in February, 1927, Mr. Lloyd, who was then assistant comptroller of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, gave evidence. He said that in five years the net earnings of the railway for eastern Canada were $76 million, and in the same period in the west the earnings were $146 million. Incidentally he said that he could not think of any operating factor that was unfavourable to western Canada in a comparison of the value of the two sections.
Reference is often made to the low freight rate in western Canada on grain and flour under the Crowsnest pass statute. Mr. Lloyd said at that time that, despite these

The Address-Mr. Maybank
rates being low, they were highly profitable. A little later, Mr. Neal, who is now president of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, said that he agreed substantially with everything that Mr. Lloyd said. He said that the Manitoba district, which runs from the head of the lakes to Broadview, Saskatchewan, was the most profitable district in the Dominion of Canada. He said that every comparison showed it to be nearest to the ideal. He also said that western Canada-that is the larger section from the lake head to the Pacific coast -was more favourable from a railwayman's point of view than the eastern part. He said that in the last four months of the year the Canadian Pacific Railway Company had moved fifty-two per cent of its total freight; that in those four months the earnings of the road were S26 million as against S15 million over the whole eight months before, and that this favourable factor was due to the western freight traffic which, as hon. members will understand, begins in the last four months of the year. He showed that the out-of-pocket expenses of the railway had been $52 million and the movement of revenue tons of freight for that amount of money had been 637,000, and that in September these revenue tons were increased two and a half times to a figure of 1,501,111 revenue tons, but the expenses went up only one million dollars. That was a case of the west paying dividends in a big way.
George Stephen, assistant freight traffic manager at that time, indicated that he was in agreement with all that had been said. From him it was learned that in 1925 the out-of-pocket railroad costs for the east were $31 million, and in the west they were $34 million; but for that difference of only $3 million there was a vastly greater amount handled in the west. For that slight difference in cost in the two sections he said they moved 8-7 billion tons in western Canada as against four billion tons in eastern Canada.
Mr. Symington also caused Mr. Stephen to show that the large net earnings over the years came from its profitable western business. The greatest proportion in earnings occurred in the last four months of 1921. Fifty per cent of the net came in the last four months. In 1922, sixty-one per cent came in that period; in the next year 65-8 per cent; in 1924 they got 59-5 per cent, and in 1925 they got 63-6 per cent. That is the story all down through the years as far as the figures carry. The earnings have been in the last four months by reason of western traffic. In other words, the west has been paying dividends in a big way over these years, despite the fact that costs have always been very
much less in carrying that business. In a period of twenty years there were $240 million of net revenue obtained in eastern Canada and $500 million obtained in western Canada.
Not only is it a fact, according to these figures, that western Canada has kept the railroad going with net revenues, but in practically every department the cost of operations was less there. We have a great many geographical disadvantages, being a long distance from tidewater being perhaps the chief, but we do have one great advantage of flat country, greater ease of building a railroad, greater ease of operating a railroad, and that is the only advantage the prairies have. An increase in freight rates tends to take away that one advantage. If other parts of the country cannot support a railroad, and1 yet a railroad is needed there, there ought to be some more equitable way of seeing that the service is given, something more equitable than imposing costs upon us who are already much more than paying our way.
In 1927 the operating costs of the Manitoba district were less than anywhere else. Mr. Lloyd said that the density of traffic out there was greater than anywhere else and that tended to reduce costs. That has always increased in favour of the west from that day on. He said that the average tons of revenue freight per loaded car mile and average tons per train mile, and the average haul were all factors more favourable in the west than in the east. He said that loadings were heavier and the average length of the train greater. Since that day, the length of the freight train has greatly increased. I know that of my own knowledge. I see trains going by now with a hundred cars. That is much more than in the years that I have mentioned. Even one hundred empty cars then was a very unusual train. The trains I see going by now are made up of cars, not of 30-ton or 40-ton capacity, but of 50-ton capacity. It is a common thing to see a hundred of them. That is the situation in western Canada. The disparity of the 1920's is greater still today. At that time the average train in western Canada consisted of 48-02 cars and, in eastern Canada, 29-20. That situation has obtained all through the years except-

A further piece of evidence showed that there were 173,000,000 freight car miles for the year in Manitoba as against 99,000,000 in Ontario.
Now, then, I did remark somewhat earlier, and somebody questioned it, that the Canadian National was not to be taken as a criterion in rate making. I believe I can indicate to the house that that is so, and I believe it is generally accepted as being the case. I believe Mr. Vaughan admitted that not very long ago in a public address. I have a large number of clippings and I am quite sure that Mr. Vaughan's statement to that effect is among them, but anyway I am quite sure it is a fact. That railroad is made up of a considerable number of lines which were built for one reason or another, very often not for economic or financial reasons. One great stretch was built for purely political reasons in connection with confederation. A whole collection of lame ducks were all shoved together and called a system. All the debts were heaped up on the new organization; and 
everybody knows the fixed charges of the Canadian National Railways are far beyond the ability of the system to pay. If the Canadian National Railways were in the United States under the interstate commerce commission it would have been run through the wringer long ago.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Your party does not agree with that.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The Soo line of the Canadian Pacific was run through the wringer long ago and of course its fixed charges when it came out were nothing like what they were when it went in.
But if the Canadian National Railways were to be considered, the story its figures would tell as respects costs and revenue in western Canada as against those in eastern Canada would foe substantially the same as that of the Canadian Pacific Railway. That railroad in 1927 handled twice as many gross tons and had twice the revenue traffic in the west as it had in the east. On one formula one might say, if it had twice as much traffic, it ought to have a cost of twice as much, but the fact is quite otherwise. The total cost in eastern Canada for a certain amount of traffic was $101,740,000 and the total cost in western Canada was $102,220,000. That is very close to an equation, although twice as much revenue traffic was handled in the west by the Canadian National as in the east.
