Mr. Speaker, the speech from the throne does not offend me, because I now realize that it was meant to be meaningless anyway. All that can be said about it is that it is a nebulous mass of verbiage with no content, a very poor legislative diet for the Canadian people. Its ineffectiveness can be surpassed only by the stand taken by the official opposition, whose intellectual bankruptcy has reached a point where they lack the faculty to disclose an alternative to the policies which they condemn.
This year has been described as year two of the atomic age, and in that respect highlights the fact that wre are living in an age of rapid change and crises. The storm warnings stand out clear and sharp. The agreed decision of the official representatives of seventeen governments at the preparatory' commission on world food proposals is that, unless the nations of the world undertake as part of their national policies a quick expansion in the production of food and goods, they will walk straight into a worse collapse than that of 1929 to 1932. The considered judgment of these representatives of seventeen governments, including those of the United Kingdom, the United States and Canada, is that, unless all nations increase consumption in an expanding economy, they' are heading for a disaster greater than that of 1929 to 1932. In the face of this, how has the Liberal government reacted? Is it pressing and leading this country into what could be economically called a dynamic economy? Perhaps it might be best described in these words:
Certainly that Liberalism which nearly a century ago moved men's hearts and minds towards ideas of freedom and social justice, towards the defence of ethical ideas and of trust in the people, has not died out. On the whole there is as much of the genuine product in the world today, perhaps more. But it has escaped from the bonds of party. It has entered into new forms and conceptions of human liberty on a world-wide scale. And nearly everywhere the parties that once embodied and expressed it, no longer do so adequately. Today, Liberal parties, if they exist at all, are fighting a rueful retreat which may not be their fault, but whatever the reason, the fact remains. There is a political moral in this and it would seem to be that in an ever-changing world parties which do not evolve new applications of their established principles find themselves superseded by those which do.

The Address-Mr. Archibald
Those are the words of an editorial in the Ottawa Citizen of February 6, under the ironic caption "Splendid Isolation".
This position of the present government was further emphasized by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) when he stated that, if capital did not industrialize the west, the people would. That, coming from a cabinet minister representing a responsible government, shows a lamentable lack of leadership in the age in which we are living, with the necessities that are staring us in the face. Yes, we must accept new principles to avert catastrophe. It is useless to speak of adequate old age pensions, adequate health insurance, and a planned immigration policy unless we revitalize our economy to show the people that we can have continually higher standards of living along with a large increase in population. The law of diminishing returns has so caught up with us that private capital will no longer take the risks necessary to develop our frontiers on the colossal scale necessary to maintain a dynamic economy. History has shown us time and time again that nations which settle back into a, state of self-complacency are wiped out and obliterated by people who require more living room. This law of the jungle is still apparent in this world today; and all the plans of standardizing arms, establishing larger national defence organizations, et cetera, will be of no avail unless we can show that we are vital and alive by having a firm growing economy in which we have complete faith.
There was a time when this country was vital and alive. When I look back through the paper of 1910, I run across these headlines: "Telegraph Line to Stewart", "Railroad at Mile 45", "Sir Ernest Shackleton heads English Company to develop the falls of the Bulkley river for power project", "Company is ready to build road from Vancouver to Alaska and confers with Premier McBride", "Mining crews go into the Groundhog coal fields", and many similar ones.
No such headlines are in our paper today, but rather the very opposite. We live in fear of depression. The events of the past year or two should be a lesson to us. We read of terrific shortages in other countries caused by the crises of war or from the lack of development during the thirties. That could very well arise in this country in the immediate future, and yet no plans or no lead is given by the government of the day to avert this condition. We read1 that four million were unemployed in Great Britain because of a shortage of coal. We, too, have suffered from a shortage of coal just in the last year, but of course not
in the same proportion. But a shortage could arise again and be of far more drastic proportions. In 1939 we spent $45'5 million on the import of coal from the United States, and in 1946 we spent 8131-2 million on importing coal from the United States. Coal is the backbone of our industrial economy even yet. If our economy is to expand, the western regions must be industrialized, especially the west coast; yet the resources of coal, the very backbone of that industrialization programme, are being depleted to the vanishing point.
The Carroll commission on coal has this to say about the two main fields on Vancouver island:
Mining has been carried on in the Nanaimo field for more than fifty years and most of the known available coal has been recovered. Recent investigations of the geological survey indicate that the reserves in the area are only sufficient to allow operations to continue at the current levels of production for from ten to fifteen years. This is confirmed by the estimates of reserves submitted by the Canadian collieries, Dunsmuir Limited. The mines in the Cumberland area have also been worked extensively and all easily available coal has been mined.
That is the position of coal mining in the two main fields on the Pacific coast. There are other fields open for development within 150 miles of tide-water and that coal is anthracite, the only anthracite in any quantity west of Pennsylvania. I am referring to the Groundhog coal field of central British Columbia.
Mr. G. S. Malloch spent some time in the Groundhog field during 1912, for the federal Department of Mines, and he made a report which can be found in the sessional papers of 1912: 26 to 26A, No. 19. On page 87 of this volume, under the heading "Character of the Coal", Mr. Malloch had this to say:
The character of the coal differs essentially from any hitherto described. It is anthracite, non-coking, and contains exceptionally high percentage of moisture. In many cases, the coal has a resinous lustre which is usually found in lignitic coal, and very likely the high moisture produces this lustre.
While in the field, he investigated the properties of the Western Development Company, the British Columbia Anthracite Syndicate and the British Columbia Anthracite Company. These companies, at that time, had claims staked in this area. In this report he has detailed data on the various seams he investigated, width of seams, moisture content, ash, fixed carbon, et cetera. He also gives descriptions of the structural geology of the area, description of the coal out-croppings and a description of the routes which a railroad would have to take to enter the field.
In 1921, evidence was given before a special committee of the House of Commons at
The Address-Mr. Archibald

Ottawa, named to inquire into the fuel supply of Canada. This evidence was given -by Mr. J. G. Scott, an official of the B.C. Skeena Coal Company, controlling 34,000 acres of anthracite coal lands situated at Groundhog mountain, British Columbia, on the head waters of the Skeena river. In appealing for aid for the development of this coal field he had this to say at one point:
I think this is a national project which is well worth the attention of parliament and if it could be realized, and I am sure that it will be realized. I believe it will cause the reproduction in northern British Columbia of all such industries as are caused by or have resulted from the development of similar classes of coal in Pennsylvania.
There are three routes by which a railway may reach the field. First, a branch northward from Hazelton on the Canadian National Railways which would follow the valley of the Skeena river, a distance of about 150 miles. Second, a route for which an independent railway once had a charter, from the mouth of the Naas river on the Pacific coast a little north of Prince Rupert to the coal field, a distance of 180 miles. The dominion government voted a subsidy of 1640.000 in 1912 to the company which was going to build a railway on this route. Third, an alternative line could be built from the -Mice Arm or Stewart on the Portland canal, a distance that way of a little over 100 miles. These are the three routes by which this coal could be moved.
Mr. Scott, further in his evidence, pointed out that just prior to the 1914-18 war, he had correspondence with Lord Rhondda, the coal baron of Great Britain, about the Groundhog coal field. Lord Rhondda was so interested in this matter that he took an interest in the company, of which Mr. Scott was a member. With the outbreak of world war I, Lord Rhondda's interest was, of course, discontinued and he died shortly afterwards.
Mr. Scott, under questioning of Mr. Douglas, then a member of parliament for Cape Breton, revealed a -report of a Mr. Gustav Grossman, a Pennsylvania engineer, who examined the field. Mr. Grossman had this to say:
During my visit to the Groundhog mountain coal field from May until October, 1912, for the purpose of investigating its economic value as far as an exhaustive superficial examination and inspection of its various exploration workings could disclose, I also examined among others, holdings of your syndicate. Without going into details as to geology, transportation facilities, et cetera, a general synopsis of the merits of your property may be given as follows, forty-seven sections, 30,080 acres, situated 56 degrees, 45 minutes north latitude and 128 degrees -15 minutes west longitude, in the west portion of the Groundhog mountain coal field, a considerable portion of which is favourably located, and 
containing coal seams of superior quality and of workable dimensions. Number of workable seams uncovered, six, with an aggregate thickness of 28 feet. Quality of the coal, anthracite, very bright and hard and of excellent steaming quality, comparing favourably with the Pennsylvania product.
Mr. Scott, further in his evidence stated:
No extraordinary or unusual engineering difficulties will be encountered in the opening up of this property, which should be capable of producing a large daily tonnage of a superior quality of fuel and I would consider the development of this group of coal claims an inviting business proposition which should be attractive to investors. There is no coal mine in the Dominion of Canada which is of the same or similar quality as this, either in physical or economic properties, and so far no such coal has been discovered in commercial quantities in the dominion. Practically speaking, there is no anthracite west of Pennsylvania in the United States. Judging by the amount of Pennsylvania anthracite that is used in the United States and Canada, it may readily be seen what a gap in the coal supply in the west will be filled by the opening of this field. The smokeless character of this coal should open for it a large market in the coastal cities, where the smoke nuisance is prohibited. Its cleanliness for household use and its steady burning properties should bring it into general use for domestic purposes. In illustrating the comparative importance of such an area as this, it may be stated that this area alone probably contains as much coal, possibly ten times as much, as is found in all the present known coal areas in -the province of Nova Scotia.
Mr. Mackenzie, then member of parliament from Nova Scotia, had this to say on the latter's statement:
I am afraid that damns that report very badly. This is a hint to you that I am from Nova Scotia.
Mr. James McEvoy, geological and mining engineer, formerly a member of the staff of the geological survey of Ottawa, had this to say:
I have no doubt that a large market can be found for this coal and at good prices. The domestic market will be the most important at first and as the coal is practically smokeless and will not make dust and dirt all over a house, as the soft coals of the west invariably do, it will be self-advertising.
The quantity of coal in this great field has not been computed. Two experienced mining engineers who examined forty-seven square miles of the territory, owned by Quebec and London capitalists, estimated that on the
30,000	acres in question there were one billion, one hundred million tons of coal.
At the present time, all licences and leases have expired in this area. There are no existing alienations. Therefore a government which is increasingly becoming concerned with the lack of industrialization in the west could afford to survey this whole area for

Barbara Ann Scott
development of its coal resources, as well as other resources that could be tied in with the development of the coal field of this area.
Our economy under present conditions consists of a series of economic islands, each functioning within itself, but deprived of its full, measure of success, owing to the lack of a balanced over-all industrial policy. Instead of our economy expanding and developing toward the maximum self-sufficiency, we are drifting more and more toward becoming a colony of the United States. This tendency must be checked and I would urge the government, as one step away from this drift, to survey and open for development such resources as are found in the Groundhog coal field. It will save needless confusion and suffering when the time comes for us once again to wake ourselves from our lethargy.
This area, known as the Groundhog region, would be intersected by the highway from Hazelton to Whitehorse, which has caused so much international conjecture, in both military and civilian circles. This Hazelton project would give access and outlet to many billions of feet of merchantable spruce and hemlock and other timber suitable for lumber and also for mining props.
The coast range carries the same geological formation on its eastern flanks, as at the Premier mine above Stewart, on its western slope. There is room for and the probability of the discovery of several Premiers, as well as the coal field that I have mentioned, on these eastern flanks, which are at present inaccessible, or practically so. Laterals from the Hazelton route would give access and outlet. The benefits to the development of this area, both as to economic resources and means of transportation, would develop great industries on the coast, and the beneficial influence would be felt from Frisco to Vancouver to Nome.
The agricultural lands of the Naas river, with its soft, healthy climate, are eminently suitable for settlement. With mining and logging underway, there would be unlimited markets for all produce. This portion of road to the Yukon and Alaska, the Hazelton-White-horse project, is a big undertaking in itself, but it is a mere gateway to infinitely vaster possibilities.
On motion of Mr. Castleden the debate was adjourned.
